name: National Iranian Oil Company
description: The National Iranian Oil Company (NIOC) is Iran’s state-owned upstream oil and natural gas company, responsible for activities associated with finding and developing hydrocarbon resources. Its institutional origins date to the nationalization of the oil industry in 1951. [s1][s2]

seo.title: National Iranian Oil Company: Origins and Upstream Role | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Understand NIOC’s origins, its role in oil and gas development, and the distinction between project announcements and operating results.

content.heading: A company rooted in oil nationalization
content.content:
The National Iranian Oil Company, usually abbreviated to NIOC, emerged from Iran’s nationalization of its oil industry in 1951. An institutional history published by China’s National Energy Administration, explicitly attributed to NIOC, traces the company’s activities to that year. It describes a broad remit spanning exploration, drilling, production, research, and the handling of petroleum products. Because that profile was published in 2018, its organizational counts and resource estimates should be read as historical statements rather than a current company inventory. [s1]

The profile also emphasizes domestic technical expertise and the development of Iranian engineering capabilities. Those statements establish the company’s account of its development; they do not independently measure technological performance, project delivery, or financial efficiency. [s1]

content.heading: Oil and gas before the distribution network
content.content:
NIOC’s central position is in the upstream industry: the activities associated with locating resources and developing producing fields. The U.S. Energy Information Administration’s institutional reference identifies it as responsible for upstream oil and natural gas projects under the wider supervision of the Ministry of Petroleum. Its role therefore includes natural gas, despite the word “Oil” in its name. [s2]

This distinction helps readers interpret company names. A gas-field development attributed to NIOC concerns a different stage of the industry from the processing and delivery functions associated with the National Iranian Gas Company. Likewise, petroleum refining and product distribution are identified separately with NIORDC. These are functional distinctions; they should not be treated as a verified contemporary map of every subsidiary or ownership relationship. [s2]

content.heading: Contracts are evidence of commitments
content.content:
The EIA’s October 2024 assessment reports that NIOC awarded additional development contracts in March 2024 for fields along the Iraqi border, including Azadegan. It also describes difficulties obtaining capital and technology for mature-field production. A contract award establishes a development commitment; it does not establish that the intended production increase subsequently occurred. [s3]

The same assessment records the partial start-up of South Pars Phase 11 in August 2023. South Pars is an offshore natural gas development in the Persian Gulf. The report distinguishes that initial operation from a later expected production plateau, illustrating why commissioning, actual output, and forecast capacity must remain separate. This page does not verify subsequent delivery against those expectations. [s3]

name: National Iranian Gas Company
description: The National Iranian Gas Company (NIGC) is a state-owned organization associated with natural gas processing, transmission, and distribution in Iran. Its network functions are institutionally distinct from the upstream field-development responsibilities described for NIOC. [s1][s2]

seo.title: National Iranian Gas Company: Processing and Networks | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: An introduction to NIGC’s gas-network responsibilities, state ownership, and the evidence needed to assess delivery performance.

content.heading: From gas resources to delivered fuel
content.content:
The National Iranian Gas Company, abbreviated to NIGC, occupies the processing and delivery side of Iran’s natural gas industry. The EIA’s institutional reference assigns it downstream gas activities, including processing and domestic distribution. This distinguishes its functions from NIOC’s upstream responsibilities for oil and gas fields. [s1]

The distinction is useful when reading reports about new projects. Developing a field and delivering usable gas through a network are different activities. An increase in resources available underground does not, by itself, demonstrate increased delivery to customers. The institutional division described by the EIA is a guide to these functions rather than proof of the current ownership of every facility. [s1]

content.heading: State ownership and corporate identity
content.content:
Global Energy Monitor’s ownership profile identifies NIGC as an Iranian legal entity headquartered in Tehran. It records the Ministry of Petroleum as its direct owner and the Government of Iran as its ultimate owner, and describes the entity as not publicly listed. This provides an ownership reference independent of the company’s own promotional material, although it is not a substitute for a current corporate registry extract. [s2]

A separate historical source is Iran’s August 2020 reply in the International Court of Justice case concerning Certain Iranian Assets. The filing describes NIGC as a state-owned public company with independent juridical status and cites its articles of association. It identifies activities including gas refining, domestic supply, exports, and supervision of the distribution network. These are representations made by Iran in litigation, not findings that the Court necessarily adopted. [s3]

content.heading: Why seasonal demand matters
content.content:
The EIA’s 2024 assessment explains that residential and commercial gas use rises in winter, while electricity-sector demand increases in summer. It identifies inadequate storage for variable seasonal demand as a system constraint. These national conditions help explain the importance of transmission and storage, but do not independently establish NIGC’s efficiency or responsibility for any particular interruption. [s4]

Evaluating network performance requires observations with clear boundaries: gas entering transmission, gas delivered to customers, and losses cannot be assumed to measure the same thing. A current assessment should establish those definitions before comparing annual totals or reporting claims of record daily delivery.

name: National Iranian Oil Refining & Distribution Company
description: The National Iranian Oil Refining & Distribution Company (NIORDC) is a state-owned organization associated with Iran’s petroleum refining and fuel-distribution system. Its documented responsibilities connect refining infrastructure with storage, petroleum pipelines, and delivery of products to the domestic market. [s1]

seo.title: NIORDC: Iran’s Petroleum Refining and Distribution Functions | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Understand NIORDC’s documented responsibilities and why refining capacity, fuel output, and domestic supply require separate evidence.

content.heading: Connecting refineries with fuel users
content.content:
The National Iranian Oil Refining & Distribution Company, abbreviated to NIORDC, belongs to the downstream petroleum system. The EIA’s institutional reference describes responsibilities covering refining and petroleum-product distribution, including refinery and storage construction, pipelines, and gasoline-station operations. [s1]

This remit differs from NIOC’s upstream field-development role and NIGC’s gas-processing and delivery functions. It concerns the infrastructure through which petroleum becomes usable fuel and reaches consumers. The functional description does not establish that NIORDC directly owns every refinery, depot, or retail outlet; a current ownership map requires facility-specific evidence. [s1]

content.heading: Refining capacity is not finished-fuel supply
content.content:
The EIA’s October 2024 assessment reports continuing gasoline imports despite expansion of Iran’s processing capacity, linking the situation to rising demand and refinery limitations. It also records the addition of a new distillation unit at Abadan in March 2023. These are national refining developments, not a consolidated measure of NIORDC’s own output or profitability. [s2]

The distinction matters when assessing investment announcements: additional processing capacity does not automatically establish an equivalent increase in gasoline available to customers. A reliable account must identify the facility, the kind of capacity being measured, and whether a reported addition has actually entered operation.

content.heading: Reading development schedules carefully
content.content:
A February 2025 refining outlook published by the Oxford Institute for Energy Studies lists South Adish and an additional Persian Gulf Star train among Iranian condensate-splitting projects associated with NIORDC. Condensate is a liquid hydrocarbon associated with gas production; it is distinguished from crude oil in refinery statistics. The outlook’s project schedule is evidence of expectations at publication, rather than confirmation of completion by the dates shown. [s3]

The EIA’s earlier assessment also describes refinery projects under construction and their expected future start-ups. Neither publication establishes their operating status at this page’s October 2026 cutoff. A current profile therefore needs commissioning records and actual throughput before presenting those projects as completed additions. [s2][s3]

content.heading: What a complete company assessment needs
content.content: NIORDC’s documented scope makes both production infrastructure and distribution infrastructure relevant to its profile. [s1] Assessing performance requires more than a list of refineries: it needs verified ownership and operating relationships, delivered product volumes, product-quality information, and evidence about transport and storage. Those items remain research requirements here rather than implied achievements.
